The core contribution is to treat truncated random walks on a graph as sentences, with nodes as words, and to learn node embeddings with a skip-gram/word2vec-style language model. Because short random walks tend to stay within densely connected communities, nodes that co-occur in walks get similar embeddings, so community structure can be recovered by clustering those embeddings. The justification rests on two parallels. First, node visitation frequencies in random walks on many real networks follow a power law, much like Zipfian word frequencies in natural language, which makes language-model machinery appropriate. Second, skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorizes a shifted pointwise mutual information matrix of node co-occurrences within a context window, so the learned representations capture random-walk proximity and hence community membership.
